summary:
Teams planning space missions will need places on Earth that closely resemble the conditions to test equipment and run trial missions. However, locating and finding these areas can be quite challenging. The GLXY Earth Analog Finder is a tool that can be used to locate sites on Earth similar to those on the Moon or Mars. First, you can select a potential site from the 20 candidates (10 for the Moon and 10 for Mars). Once you have made your selection, you can use the tuners in the next step to customize which specific 11 features (such as temperature, terrain, remoteness, and more) you care about the most. Our website ranks over 800 areas on Earth, narrowing it down to the top 35 most similar sites on Earth to your chosen location. It provides you with detailed site descriptions, information, NASA imagery, elevation, and direct comparison to the location you picked on either the Moon or Mars.
Our data pulls from a variety of Space Agency sources, such as terrain and temperature from LRO and MGS, the climate from NASA POWER, and more. This data is used to create estimates that compare the Earth site to the actual area. Our website searches across every part of the Earth, meaning it can help to find lesser-known analogs. Some characteristics are impossible to reproduce on Earth, such as the gravity, vacuum, or radiation of the planets.
We hope our website can be used to further accelerate the processes needed to take people to the Moon, and eventually Mars in the future!
details: Our project is a website designed to find places on Earth that share similarities with some specific locations found on the Moon or Mars. It is very easy to use, with its step-based design, and is very rich in information and data. We hope our project will be used to identify potential Earth analogs of the Moon or Mars fairly efficiently. Our biggest tool was Claude, an AI developed by Anthropic, which coded our website using a blend of HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. Our project is creative in the fact that our team considered that choosing from a select number of well-known sites on Earth was not a good idea, since our project wouldn't be doing anything new. Therefore, we decided to look across the Earth by partitioning it into a grid of 5°x 5° squares, where only the squares with center points on land were counted. Alongside 16 small (1° x 1°) named sites, we had a total of 822 areas to analyze and choose from (only the top 35 are displayed on the website).
